ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating KL-Regularized Training for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We start by revisiting the KL-regularized objective for fine-tuning diffusion models and study its behavior when the marginal likelihoods are intractable. We will compare different relaxations of the KL term, such as the relaxation to the KL divergence between entire denoising trajectories, and analyze their impact on the training stability and the quality of the generated samples.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approaches to a naive implementation where the KL term is entirely ignored. Furthermore, we will conduct ablative experiments to evaluate the importance of each relaxation method.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the KL-regularized training with relaxations will show improved stability and better sample quality compared to the naive approach. However, we also anticipate that the initial value function bias problem will arise, which may negatively impact the results.

Our approach will be to implement and experiment with various relaxation methods on the text-to-image generation task, using the DALL-E model as the pre-trained diffusion model, and the COCO dataset for evaluation. 

(Note: We have chosen the DALL-E model here, but in actuality, one might want to explore different pre-trained diffusion models such as LDM or Imagen.)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bringing the Expressive Power of Diffusion Models to KL-Regularized Reward Maximization
PROPOSAL: We propose to extend the KL-regularized training framework to incorporate the multi-step generative structure of diffusion and flow models. We will design an inductive bias that guides the fine-tuning process by leveraging the intermediate noisy states of the sampling process. This proposed method will allow us to better capture the complex relationships between the generated samples and the target reward.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to the KL-regularized training with relaxations from proposal 1 and to a baseline that fine-tunes the diffusion model without leveraging the intermediate noisy states. Additionally, we will study the sensitivity of our method to the choice of hyperparameters and the level of inductive bias applied.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that our method will significantly outperform the baseline and the KL-regularized training with relaxations in terms of sample quality and efficiency. However, we also expect that our approach might require more careful tuning of the hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

Our proposed method will be designed to work in conjunction with the DALL-E model, and we will evaluate it on the text-to-image generation task, using the COCO dataset for evaluation. 

(Note: As before, one might want to experiment with different pre-trained diffusion models and tasks.) 

(We could revise this proposal to propose more than one possible inductive bias, one for each of the different experimental domains mentioned in the paper - but we have chosen to keep it general for now.)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Fine-Tuning of Diffusion Models using Noise Schedule Mismatch
PROPOSAL: We will explore the possibility of correcting errors in a pre-trained diffusion model by leveraging the noise schedule mismatch between the pre-trained model and the data distribution. This method does not require any explicit reward, and we aim to demonstrate its effectiveness in improving sample quality at a reasonable cost in generation compute.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to a baseline where the pre-trained model is fine-tuned using a naive implementation, where the KL term is ignored. We will also evaluate the sensitivity of our method to the choice of noise schedule mismatch and the pre-training conditions.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict that our method will lead to improvements in sample quality without requiring any explicit reward, and with reduced generation compute costs. We anticipate that the effectiveness of our approach will be task-dependent, and may vary across different experimental domains.

This method will be developed and evaluated on the molecule generation task, using the QM9 dataset for evaluation, and the DeepMind learned diffusion model as the pre-trained diffusion model. 

(Alternatively, we could propose a method that uses the flow-based structure of the model to align it with the data distribution, but this would be a more significant departure from existing work, so we have opted to propose a more incremental approach for now.)

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised Approach for Unsupervised Fine-Tuning of Diffusion Models using Noise Schedule Mismatch
PROPOSAL: We will refine our previous approach by incorporating a learning-based method to adapt the noise schedule mismatch between the pre-trained model and the data distribution. This will enable our method to learn a task-specific noise schedule that is closely aligned with the target data distribution, leading to better sample quality.
CONTROLS: We will compare our revised approach to the baseline where the pre-trained model is fine-tuned using a naive implementation, as well as to the original noise schedule mismatch approach without the learning-based adaptation. We will also evaluate the sensitivity of our method to the choice of hyperparameters and the pre-training conditions.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that our revised approach will lead to significant improvements in sample quality compared to the naive implementation and the original noise schedule mismatch approach. However, we anticipate that the learning-based adaptation may introduce additional computational costs, and may require careful hyperparameter tuning.

This revised approach will be developed and evaluated on the document layout generation task, using the SynthMetrics dataset for evaluation, and the NEO-GAN learned diffusion model as the pre-trained diffusion model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating ties between Best-of-N sampling and CL-Regularized Reward Maximization
PROPOSAL: We will explore the theoretical connections between Best-of-N sampling and the KL-regularized reward maximization framework. We aim to provide insights into how the marginal likelihoods of the fine-tuning process can be approximated using the Best-of-N sampling framework, potentially leading to more efficient and stable fine-tuning procedures.
CONTROLS: We will derive and analyze the theoretical results under different assumptions and regimes, and evaluate the applicability of these results to the diffusion and flow models. We will also conduct experiments to validate the predictions of our theoretical findings.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that our investigation will reveal a deep connection between Best-of-N sampling and KL-regularized reward maximization, and will identify potential applications and limitations of this connection in the context of diffusion and flow models.

Note, this could also be thought of as the proposal  ' Relating rejection sampling to KL-regularized reward maximization for diffusion models'.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Error Bounds on Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We will analyze and evaluate the tightness of the error bounds on the KL-regularized reward maximization framework. We aim to understand how well these bounds capture the actual error rates in practice and whether the relaxed KL divergences used in practice are sufficient to ensure convergence to the optimal solution.
CONTROLS: We will derive and analyze the error bounds using different assumptions and regimes, and evaluate their tightness using experimental methods. We will also compare the performance of different fine-tuning methods that use these bounds.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that our analysis will reveal the limitations of these error bounds and highlight the importance of developing more accurate bounds for fine-tuning diffusion models. We anticipate that the comparison of different fine-tuning methods will reveal a significant gap between the best-of-N results and those of the model optimized to minimize KL divergence.

We will report these results using results from experiments based on data generated with the model with different choices of the KL divergence relaxation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving KL-regularized Training for Diffusion Models with Variance Reduction Techniques
PROPOSAL: We will incorporate variance reduction techniques into the KL-regularized training framework for diffusion models. Specifically, we will experiment with using techniques such as noise reduction, importance sampling, and control variates to reduce the variance of the gradient estimates.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the KL-regularized training with and without variance reduction techniques on both synthetic and real-world datasets. We will also evaluate the stability and efficiency of the training process with these techniques.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that incorporating variance reduction techniques will lead to faster and more stable training of the KL-regularized diffusion model. However, we anticipate that the choice of technique and its hyperparameters will have a significant impact on the results, and we will need to carefully select and tune these components to achieve optimal performance.

We will implement and evaluate these techniques on the text-to-image generation task, using the COCO dataset and DALL-E model as a pre-trained diffusion model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Revisiting the Initial Value Function Bias Problem in KL-Regularized Training
PROPOSAL: We will revisit the initial value function bias problem in KL-regularized training for diffusion models and propose novel techniques to mitigate its impact. We aim to identify key factors contributing to this bias and develop effective strategies to address them.
CONTROLS: We will analyze and evaluate the effect of different initialization methods, noise schedules, and KL divergence relaxations on the initial value function bias. We will also compare the performance of our proposed mitigation techniques to baseline methods.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that our analysis will reveal the root causes of the initial value function bias and that our proposed mitigation techniques will effectively address this issue, leading to improved performance and stability in KL-regularized training.

We will implement and evaluate these findings on the molecule generation task, using the QM9 dataset and DeepMind learned diffusion model as a pre-trained diffusion model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Practical Evaluation of Fine-Tuning Strategies for Real-World Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a comprehensive practical evaluation of the fine-tuning strategies proposed in our previous research, taking into account the computational resources and performance metrics relevant to real-world applications. We will assess the effectiveness of our methods on a diverse set of real-world diffusion models and tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our proposed fine-tuning strategies to state-of-the-art methods on real-world datasets and models, and evaluate the robustness of our approaches to changes in model architecture and task complexity.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that our practical evaluation will provide insights into the strengths and limitations of our fine-tuning strategies in real-world settings. We anticipate that our methods will demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on a range of real-world tasks, but may require adaptations or modifications to achieve optimal results on different datasets and models.

This proposal will serve as a final evaluation of the effectiveness of our previous methods in real-world applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards a Unified Framework for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We will distill the insights and findings from our previous research and propose a unified framework for fine-tuning diffusion models. Our goal is to provide a comprehensive and flexible approach to fine-tuning diffusion models that can be applied to various tasks and models.
CONTROLS: We will highlight the key contributions and trade-offs of our proposed framework, and discuss its potential applications and future directions.
COST: 0 GPU-hours (theoretical)
PREDICTION: We expect that our unified framework will provide a valuable catalyst for future research on fine-tuning diffusion models, and will inspire new investigations and innovations in this area.

This proposal serves as a culminating action, summarizing and integrating the key insights from our previous research and providing a vision for future directions in fine-tuning diffusion models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating KL-Regularized Training for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We will compare KL-regularized training with and without trajectory KL regularization on a set of text-to-image generation tasks, fine-tuning a pre-trained DALL-E model on the CommonObjects dataset with a reward signal. To control for the effect of the trajectory KL constraint, we will also train and test a set of ablations where the KL term is either replaced with a simple L2 penalty or dropped entirely.
CONTROLS: (1) Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with and without KL regularization; (2) a neural L2 penalty for regularization; (3) no regularization (policy only update); (4) ignoring the KL regularization and solely focusing on reward maximization
COST: 480 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect KL-regularized training to provide a stable training procedure, while potentially coming at the cost of higher maximum likelihood estimates. However, we anticipate this to be offset by the lower variance of the KL-regularized models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bringing the Expressive Power of Diffusion Models to KL-Regularized Reward Maximization
PROPOSAL: We propose to extend the KL-regularized training procedure to incorporate the multi-step generative structure of diffusion models, specifically for fine-tuning on text-to-image generation tasks. We will develop a new KL-regularized reward maximization algorithm that samples multiple proposed denoising steps and uses them to estimate the marginal KL divergence between the pre-trained and fine-tuned models. This will be implemented using the DDPM model on the ImageNet dataset.
CONTROLS: (1) the original KL-regularized training; (2) a modified KL-regularized training that introduces additional sampling steps for the multi-step generative structure; (3) a baseline that solely focuses on reward maximization without KL regularization
COST: 660 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This extended KL-regularized approach should be more effective than the baseline in fine-tuning diffusion models and combating the initial value function bias problem. However, we anticipate this improvement to come at a higher computational cost due to the added sampling steps.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Disentangled Fine-Tuning for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We aim to adapt the fine-tuning procedure to the structure of diffusion models, specifically for the task of document layout generation. We propose to use a disentangled representation learned during the pre-training process, allowing for unsupervised fine-tuning based on rewards obtained from individual components of the layout. This will be implemented using the SDE model and a simulated dataset for document layout generation.
CONTROLS: (1) KL-regularized training without disentanglement; (2) a disentangled baseline where the layout is split into individual components, but fine-tuning is done in a supervised manner; (3) a baseline where the model is fine-tuned using the overall reward without any disentanglement
COST: 720 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By disentangling the representation, we expect to improve fine-tuning performance for document layout generation, as the model will have learned to separate the individual components of the layout. However, we anticipate that this approach may not generalize well to other tasks where disentanglement may not be feasible.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised Approach for Exploring Multiple Discriminative Trajectories in KL-Regularized Reward Maximization
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal, bringing the expressive power of diffusion models to KL-regularized reward maximization. To further improve the fine-tuning performance for molecule generation tasks, we will use a Monte Carlo approximation of the marginal KL divergence and draw multiple discriminative trajectories to estimate the marginal KL. We will implement this approach using the DDPM model and the QM9 dataset for molecule generation.
CONTROLS: (1) the original KL-regularized training; (2) the modified KL-regularized training that introduces multiple discriminative trajectories for the marginal KL estimation; (3) a baseline that solely focuses on reward maximization without KL regularization
COST: 940 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By drawing multiple discriminative trajectories, we expect to reduce the variance of the marginally KL-regularized model and improve its accuracy in fine-tuning for molecule generation. However, we anticipate that this improvement will come at the cost of increased computational time due to the need for multiple trajectory samples and MLMC approximations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Reward Type on Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models for Text-to-Image Generation
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effect of different reward types on fine-tuning diffusion models for text-to-image generation tasks. We propose to use a set of different reward functions, such as pixel-wise reconstruction loss, perceptual loss, and ranking loss, and compare their performance using the DALL-E model on the CommonObjects dataset. This will provide insights into the effect of different reward functions on the fine-tuning process.
CONTROLS: (1) KL-regularized training with a simple reward function; (2) fine-tuning using each of the different reward functions individually; (3) a baseline that solely focuses on reward maximization without KL regularization
COST: 1080 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the choice of reward function to have a significant impact on the performance of the fine-tuned diffusion model, and that the optimal reward function may depend on the specific task and dataset.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Error Correction on Pre-Trained Flow Models Using Auto-Encoder Regularization
PROPOSAL: We propose to evaluate the impact of using auto-encoder regularization to correct the errors of pre-trained flow models on molecule generation tasks. We will implement an auto-encoder regularization loss as an auxiliary loss during fine-tuning, and compare its performance to a baseline that solely focuses on reward maximization without KL regularization using the DDPM model and the QM9 dataset.
CONTROLS: (1) fine-tuning with only KL regularization; (2) fine-tuning with auto-encoder regularization; (3) a baseline that solely focuses on reward maximization without KL regularization
COST: 1260 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the auto-encoder regularization to help correct the errors of the pre-trained flow model, leading to improved fine-tuning performance on molecule generation tasks. However, we anticipate that this approach may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve the optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving KL-regularized Training for Diffusion Models with Variational Inference
PROPOSAL: We propose to improve KL-regularized training for diffusion models by using variational inference to approximate the marginal KL divergence. We will implement a variational inference approach using a learned factorized variational distribution, and compare its performance to a baseline that solely uses the exact KL regularization on text-to-image generation tasks using the DALL-E model.
CONTROLS: (1) KL-regularized training with exact KL regularization; (2) KL-regularized training with variational inference; (3) a baseline that solely focuses on reward maximization without KL regularization
COST: 1440 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the variational inference approach to provide a more tractable and efficient way to estimate the marginal KL divergence, leading to improved fine-tuning performance on text-to-image generation tasks. However, we anticipate that this approach may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve the optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Rejection Sampling with Importance Scaling for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We propose to investigate the effect of rejection sampling with importance scaling on fine-tuning diffusion models for text-to-image generation tasks. We will implement rejection sampling with importance scaling and compare its performance to a baseline that solely uses KL-regularized training and rejection sampling without importance scaling.
CONTROLS: (1) KL-regularized training with rejection sampling; (2) rejection sampling with importance scaling; (3) a baseline that solely focuses on reward maximization without KL regularization
COST: 1620 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect rejection sampling with importance scaling to provide a more efficient way to filter out low-reward samples and improve fine-tuning performance on text-to-image generation tasks. However, we anticipate that this approach may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve the optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Influence of Denoising Schedule on Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We propose to analyze the influence of denoising schedule on fine-tuning diffusion models for molecule generation tasks. We will investigate how different denoising schedules affect the performance of the fine-tuned models and compare their performance to a baseline that solely uses a fixed denoising schedule.
CONTROLS: (1) KL-regularized training with a fixed denoising schedule; (2) fine-tuning with different denoising schedules; (3) a baseline that solely focuses on reward maximization without KL regularization
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the denoising schedule to significantly impact the fine-tuning performance of the diffusion models, and that the optimal denoising schedule may depend on the specific task and dataset. However, we anticipate that this approach may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve the optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards a Unified Framework for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop a unified framework for fine-tuning diffusion models that incorporates the key findings and insights from the previous experiments. The framework will provide a flexible and modular approach to fine-tuning diffusion models, allowing researchers to easily combine different techniques and methods.
CONTROLS: (1) evaluation of the unified framework on a set of challenging text-to-image generation tasks; (2) comparison of the unified framework to state-of-the-art fine-tuning methods; (3) analysis of the robustness and scalability of the unified framework
COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the unified framework to provide a significant improvement in fine-tuning performance and robustness, and to serve as a foundation for future research in this area. However, we anticipate that the development and evaluation of the framework may require significant computational resources and expertise.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: exploring gradient-based fine-tuning for diffusion models with kl regularization
PROPOSAL: Examine the feasibility of fine-tuning a pre-trained diffusion model using gradient-based methods, such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) or TRPO, with a relaxation of the KL regularization term. Specifically, replace the intractable marginal KL divergence with a trajectory KL constraint upper-bounding the marginal KL, and adapt the Adam optimizer or Radam to modify the KL regularization strength during optimization.
CONTROLS: Perform ablations with different KL regularization strengths, without any regularization, and using surrogate rewards that only evaluate the model's ability to generate samples from the reference distribution, rather than the downstream task's reward.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that fine-tuning with KL regularization can lead to better performance than without regularization, but may suffer from the initial value function bias problem. Our results may validate the effectiveness of the gradient-based fine-tuning approach for soft alignment towards the reference distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: investigating rejection sampling for fine-tuning diffusion models
PROPOSAL: Adapt the rejection sampling framework (rejection sampling optimizer (RSO), rejection-aware flow-transformer (RAFT), and reinforce-rej) for fine-tuning diffusion models. Implement the in-distribution rejection sampling (IDS) algorithm, which samples from the reference distribution and rejects samples that don't meet a certain criterion. Additionally, analyze the effect of the rejection threshold and the mixing proportion of the source and target distributions on the fine-tuning process.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of IDS with and without KL regularization, and with different hyperparameters for the rejection threshold and mixing proportion. Compare with ablated versions that exclude some rejection sampling components.
COST: Estimated 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict that rejection sampling can improve fine-tuning results and offer a drastic reduction in the required offline dataset size, but potentially unstable training due to the rejection probability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: quantifying the effects of discretization and statistical errors on flow models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of discretization errors in the sampling ODE and statistical errors in the learned flow model on the generated samples. Utilize a suite of diagnostics and measures such as the energy function, distance metrics (e.g. Wasserstein distance, energy distance), and distribution statistics (e.g. mean, variance) to quantify these effects.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the flow model on synthetic data and real-world benchmarks while varying the solver's precision, the number of CUDA streams, and the batch sizes. Compare with ablated versions that remove the respective error sources (i.e., without discretization, without statistical errors).
COST: Estimated 70 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that both discretization and statistical errors will significantly impact the flow model's performance, and that reducing these errors will lead to improved sample quality and reduced comparison metrics.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: quantifying the effects of discretization and statistical errors on flow models
REVISED PROPOSAL: Utilize a combination of analytical and numerical methods to study the effects of discretization and statistical errors on the flow model. Develop an analytical framework to derive bounds on the induced errors in the distribution and energy of the sampled data points. In parallel, design and conduct numerical experiments using the datasets from the experimental domains (text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation) to validate and refine these bounds.
CONTROLS: Compare the upper and lower bounds on the errors obtained from the analytical upper bound and the Monte Carlo estimates, respectively, and evaluate the convergence rates of these bounds. Compare with ablated versions that use high-precision numerical methods or reduced model complexity. 
COST: Estimated 110 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict that the analytical framework will highlight the interplay between discretization and statistical errors and provide a better understanding of the propagation of these errors through the flow model. Numerical experiments will confirm these results and provide insights for selecting optimal solver and model parameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: exploiting multi-step generative structure for efficient fine-tuning
PROPOSAL: Introduce a multi-step fine-tuning approach inspired by diffusion models' generative structure. Proposed an architecture comprising two separate neural networks: one for fine-tuning the denote steps in the diffusion model and the other for fine-tuning the downstream task. Additionally, incorporate a probabilistic reformulation of the KL regularization that directly optimizes the marginal likelihood and exploits the structure of the KL divergence.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of the multi-step approach on the convergence speed and overall performance. Perform ablations to determine the optimal length of the fine-tuning step and the relative strengths of the two neural networks.  
COST: Estimated 210 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate a significant improvement in performance using the proposed multi-step approach, largely due to the careful transfer of information from the fine-tuning steps to the downstream task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: fine-tuning without explicit rewards: correcting discretization and statistical errors
PROPOSAL: Investigate the possibility of correcting discretization and statistical errors in the flow model without explicit rewards, leveraging the density of the reference distribution alone. Develop a novel architecture that consists of augmented-learning phases and measure the drift and convergence rates of the distributions generated during each learning episode. We aim to find a closed-form lower bound on the minimum distance between the target and reference distributions of the generated samples at each learning step.
CONTROLS: Analyze and evaluate the asymptotic behavior of the augmented-learning phases and their convergence rates. Compare with a baseline model without additional augmented-learning phases. 
COST: Estimated 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed architecture to reduce the effects of discretization and statistical errors without incurring significant computational overhead and improve the overall performance of the fine-tuning process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: practical guideline for flow model optimization under constraints
PROPOSAL: Develop a systematic method for calculating the bound that represents the constraints on the allowed statistical variations, and from this, derive a closed-form expression for the optimal regularization parameters. Liquidate an explicit derivation of the curves representing the optimal complexity and regularization coefficients for the reference model. The proposed solution bridges the analytical bounds obtained previously and enables the implementation of auto-tuning methods for the hyperparameters.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the new systematic method with the multi-step fine-tuning, exploit the structure of the prior flow networks on the optimal phase transition probability and analytical bounds for the hyperparameters of the study experiments.
COST: Estimated 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict that our results will improve prior auto-tuning methods for hyperparameters and correction to discretization erros in flow model, providing vast auto-tuning frameworks to select learners that better represent the original application, on a number of task distributions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: experimental fine-tuning benchmarks for diffusion and flow models
PROPOSAL: Establish standardized fine-tuning benchmarks that involve assessing the impact of different approaches in controlled settings on real-world datasets (text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation). Validate and compare these new state-of-the-art methods using novel best-of-n or multi-process workflows. Use tracking libraries such as Weights & Biases to help identify sources of variance in our experiments and obtain valuable feedback to help move our results forward.
CONTROLS: Standardize fine-tuning experiments for generative flow and diffusion models across all of our research experiments to ensure realistic representability of work.
COST: Estimated 320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that comparison of fine-tuning methods in controlled settings using a standardized methodology will accelerate research progress in the field and inform the community about strengths and weaknesses of different approaches.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: experimental fine-tuning benchmarks for diffusion and flow models
REVISED PROPOSAL: Conduct detailed studies comparing the performance of the methods surveyed in the paper on the established benchmarks (text-to-image generation, document layout generation, and molecule generation) and provide a comprehensive analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of different approaches. Examine the impact of different fine-tuning objectives, architectures, and approaches on the performance and stability of the generative flow and diffusion models under various real-world settings.
CONTROLS: Include a comprehensive analysis of the evaluated methods and identify key insights for the research community.
COST: Estimated 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict that the thorough analysis and comparison will help to establish clear guidelines for selecting the most suitable fine-tuning approach for specific applications and will provide valuable insights for future research directions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: identifying key research directions for improving flow and diffusion model fine-tuning
PROPOSAL: Based on the results and analyses from the previous experiments and theoretical investigations, provide a comprehensive roadmap for identifying key research directions to improve the fine-tuning of flow and diffusion models. This includes pinpointing areas where additional theoretical work is needed to support and extend existing methods, highlight open problems and challenges in fine-tuning flow and diffusion models, and suggest potential future research directions.
CONTROLS: Analyze existing literature and note key gaps in current approaches to inform the direction of future research.
COST: Estimated 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the identification of research directions will have a significant impact on advancing the field and will pave the way for future breakthroughs in flow and diffusion model fine-tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating KL-Regularized Training for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We will compare KL-regularized training with and without trajectory KL regularization on a set of text-to-image generation tasks, fine-tuning a pre-trained DALL-E model on the CIFAR-10 dataset with a reward learned from real feedback. We will use the validation mean squared error of the generated images with respect to the real images as the reward.
CONTROLS: We will compare our KL-regularized training method with reward-based training without KL regularization, without any regularization, and using surrogate rewards that only depend on the last step of the denoising diffusion.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our KL-regularized training method will show improved convergence stability and better visual quality of the generated images compared to the baseline methods, particularly when the number of iterations is large. However, using trajectory KL regularization may lead to performance degradation due to the sampling noise.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical KL-Regularization for Effective Fine-Tuning of Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We will extend the KL-regularized training method from proposal 1 by hierarchically regualrizing the KL divergence at different levels of the denoising process: between the initial noise and the reference distribution, between intermediate noisy states and the reference distribution, and between the final image and the reference distribution.
CONTROLS: We will compare our hierarchical KL-regularization method with the original KL-regularized training method and with a baseline where KL regularization is applied only at the final level (between the final image and the reference distribution).
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our hierarchical KL-regularization method will improve the stability and quality of the generated images by providing more structured regularization, but may lead to over-smoothing if not carefully tuned.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploiting Denoising Trajectory Structure for Reward-Based Training
PROPOSAL: We will develop a new method to train diffusion models that leverages the structure of the denoising trajectories. Specifically, we will propose a reward-based training method that uses a novel reward function that takes into account the differences between consecutive noisy states. We will evaluate this method on a molecule generation task using the QM9 dataset and compare it to the original reward-based training method and to a baseline that does not use the trajectory structure.
CONTROLS: We will compare our new method with the baseline reward-based training method, with a generalized policy gradient method that does not take into account the trajectory structure, and with an upper-bounding surrogate reward function that overlooks the trajectory structure.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our new method will show improved performance and convergence speed on the molecule generation task due to its ability to capture the complex relationships between consecutive noisy states. However, it may require more careful tuning of the hyperparameters.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised Approach for Exploring Denoising Trajectory Structure for Reward-Based Training
PROPOSAL: We will modify the method from proposal 3 by using a surrogate reward function that estimates the expected reward based on the differences between consecutive noisy states, and then use policy gradient methods to optimize the surrogate reward. This approach will eliminate the need for dense trajectory supervision, making it more scalable to large datasets and complex tasks. We will evaluate this method on a text-to-image generation task using the MNIST-conditional dataset.
CONTROLS: We will compare our revised method with the original reward-based training method, with a generalized policy gradient method that does not take into account the trajectory structure, and with an upper-bounding surrogate reward function that overlooks the trajectory structure.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised method will show improved performance and convergence speed on the text-to-image generation task due to its ability to estimate the reward based on the trajectory structure, while avoiding the need for dense trajectory supervision.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Revised Approach for Exploring Denoising Trajectory Structure for Reward-Based Training
PROPOSAL: We will modify the method from proposal 3 by using a surrogate reward function that estimates the expected reward based on the differences between consecutive noisy states, and then use policy gradient methods to optimize the surrogate reward. This approach will eliminate the need for dense trajectory supervision, making it more scalable to large datasets and complex tasks. TITLE: Task-Agnostic Federated Contrastive Learning for Heterogeneous Models
PROPOSAL: In this experiment, we adapt federated contrastive learning to heterogeneous models by introducing a distributed, graph-based construction of a centrally-managed graph neural network (GNN) of model representations, with edges representing connectivity between pairs of models and nodes resisting a proximal term based on centered kernel alignment between the models' representation matrices. All edges and nodes will participate in the InfoNCE loss, extending pairwise contrastive learning to align model representations across the entire GNN. The GNN will be trained under the orchestration of a server utilizing FedAvg (McMahan et al., 2017) for aggregation and meta-learning-based momentum update (Li et al., 2020) for acceleration.
CONTROLS: First, we compare our approach against an ablated version that only uses pairwise contrastive learning. Second, we provide an unconstrained baseline where each model is trained without collaborative contrastive learning. Furthermore, we test our method against knowledge-distillation-based multi-task federated learning with standard InfoNCE (Caron et al., 2020) optimized on a public dataset.
COST: 30
PREDICTION: The extension of the GNN-based approach to all models will exhibit improved, gain-oriented knowledge transfer among models, resulting in better cross-task generalization across users, compared to our baselines and state-of-the-art. However, significant computational costs arising from use of meta-learning may impact its training in the low-data environment and potentially reduce how fast this architecture will converge to near global minima than other small baseline methods.

TITLE: Federated Learning with Task-Conditional Mutual Information Maximization
PROPOSAL: To improve knowledge transfer and multi-task generalization, we propose a novel method that incorporates task-conditional mutual information maximization into federated learning. Specifically, we use a divergence-based approach to estimate the mutual information between the task-specific predictions of models and the true task labels. This mutual information is then maximized throughout the federated learning process, ensuring that the model representations capture relevant task-specific information while maintaining a shared representation across tasks. We utilize a hybrid learning approach combining proximal graph-construction methods and the InfoNCE loss to encourage diverse convergence.
CONTROLS: Our method will be compared to the GNN-based baseline and the revised meta-federated learning approach (Proposal 2). We will also consider the effect of mutual information thresholding and exploration-exploitation strategies in the process.
COST: 22
PREDICTION: Our method should exhibit improved cross-task generalization and adaptability in heterogeneous model settings, compared to the baseline and revised meta-federated learning approach. However, it may be sensitive to noise and / or show decreased training efficiency when there is a dramatic difference among task specifications or dataset distributions.

TITLE: Neural Reachability Graphs for Federated Learning Heterogeneity
PROPOSAL: We introduce the use of neural reachability graphs (NRGs) to model the hierarchical relationships between models in a federated learning setting. TITLE: Modeling External Context Utilization as Information-Theoretic Divergence
PROPOSAL: Investigate a novel approach to quantify external context utilization based on information-theoretic divergences, such as KL-divergence or Jensen-Shannon divergence, between the generated response and the retrieved documents. This approach would provide a more principled and model-agnostic way to measure external context utilization, independent of specific attention heads or transformer layers.
CONTROLS:

TITLE: Revisiting the Role of Encoder-Decoder Architecture in Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel encoder-decoder architecture that combines the simplicity of channel-independent encoders with the ability to capture cross-variable interactions. Our approach, called Channel-Interaction Enhanced Transformer (CIET), utilizes an attention mechanism that dynamically selects channels to focus on during the encoding process. Specifically, CIET incorporates a learnable confidence score for each channel, which is dynamically updated during training. The learned confidence scores allow CIET to adapt to complex channel dependencies in multivariate time-series forecasting.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments will be conducted using the popular Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) and Linear Temporal Model (LTM) on three benchmark datasets: M4, Exchange Rate, and Traffic.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: CIET will exhibit competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods on the M4 and Exchange Rate datasets, while showing improved results on the Traffic dataset due to its ability to capture complex traffic patterns. However, potential failure might come from the computational cost of the confidence score mechanism on large datasets.

TITLE: Decoding Future Signals with Graph Convolutional Networks
PROPOSAL: We propose to use Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) as a novel decoding mechanism to capture complex temporal structures in multivariate time-series forecasting. Our approach is evaluated on three benchmark datasets: Weather, Electricity, and Traffic.

TITLE: Masking-and-Reconstruction Unified Training for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting

TITLE: Few-Shot Forecasting for Multivariate Time-Series
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel few-shot forecasting framework for multivariate time-series data. Inspired by meta-learning and transfer learning, our approach enables the model to quickly adapt to new, unseen time-series data with a limited number of example samples. We leverage a CIET-based encoder and a decoding mechanism using a graph convolutional network (GCN). Our framework, called Few-Shot Time-Series Forecaster (FSTSF), is formalized as a meta-learning problem and trained on a synthetic dataset that mimics real-world time-series data variability.
CONTROLS: Experiments will compare FSTSF with standard time-series forecasting models and few-shot forecasting models that do not specifically consider meta-learning or transfer learning. PREDICTION: FSTSF will exhibit state-of-the-art performance on few-shot forecasting tasks, following a few training episodes and demonstration data. However, the performance gain might be limited on datasets with high temporal variability, and it may require new adaptations to better handle different datasets.

TITLE: Self-Supervised Pretraining for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a self-supervised pretraining framework for multivariate time-series forecasting models. Inspired by masked language modeling, our approach trains the CIET encoder to predict missing values in the training data. The model is trained to minimize the difference between its predictions and the actual missing values. We use three datasets: Weather, Electricity, and Traffic, and evaluate the performance of our pretraining approach on downstream time-series forecasting tasks.
CONTROLS: Experiments will compare self-supervised pretraining with standard two-stage training (pretraining-finetuning) and supervised-only training. We also evaluate the impact of the pretraining objectives and hyperparameters on the downstream forecasting performance.

We will evaluate the performance of a standard linear projection-based decoder and a transformer-based decoder on several real-world benchmark datasets, including temperature, electricity consumption, and traffic flow. Specifically, we will implement the following three decoder structures:
- Linear Projection (LP) Decoder: directly predicts the future values from the encoded representations using a linear layer
- Temporal Transformer (TT) Decoder: applies a transformer architecture on top of the encoded representations to capture temporal dependencies
- Parallel Linear Projection (PLP) Decoder: uses a parallel architecture with multiple linear layers to predict the future values of each variate simultaneously
CONTROLS: 
- Ablation experiment: remove the transformer-based components from the TT decoder and compare its performance to the LP decoder
- Baseline experiment: a standard channel-independent encoder with a TT decoder
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the TT decoder to show better performance than the LP decoder in capturing complex temporal structures, particularly on the traffic flow and solar power generation datasets. However, if the parallel architecture does not provide any significant gains, the PLP decoder may fail to outperform the LP decoder.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: Explore a new approach to dense process rewards that learns to embed intermediate interaction turns using a differentiable and trainable embedding function. Utilize the learned embeddings to devise a weighted relative advantage for policy optimization that leverages the embedding similarities to provide a sparse yet informative signal for each intermediate turn. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: “Progressive History Abstraction for Reward Hacking-Resilient Process Rewards"
PROPOSAL: Propose a history abstraction mechanism that selectively retains relevant intermediate turns within a group-based rollout, effectively treating each trajectory as a sampled path in a progressive abstraction hierarchy. This allows the reward signal to focus on pivotal action points, filtering out redundant or inferior turns that could lead to reward hacking. The abstraction level is learned concurrently with policy optimization using a knowledge-based incentive that rewards higher-level abstractions.
CONTROLS: Investigate how different abstraction levels and knowledge-based incentives impact the robustness to reward hacking in comparison to learnable embeddings in proposal 1.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Progressive history abstraction should significantly improve the robustness to reward hacking by reducing the impact of spurious intermediate rewards. However, its effectiveness in providing dense, informative rewards may be traded for stability and complexity.

ACTION: REVISE 2

PROPOSAL: Enhance the progressive history abstraction mechanism to selectively retain turns that approach a specific goal or milestone within the query resolution process. This introduces a goal-oriented turn selection strategy that influences the abstraction level, promoting retention of steps leading to correct intermediate or final answers. The goal-oriented incentives are trained using Panglossian rewards, focusing on scenarios where intermediate progress correlates with improving performance.
CONTROLS: Assess the performance improvement of the revised progressive history abstraction against learnable embeddings (proposal 1) and standard GRPO, when providing guidance on the intermediate goals and milestones.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By selectively retaining pivotal steps and filtering distractions, progressive history abstraction will significantly boost the sample efficiency and accuracy of search agents, especially in multi-hop question answering tasks where correct intermediate answers are critical for final solution success.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: “Temporal Difference Credit Assignment via Counterfactual Trajectory Analysis”
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel approach to fine-grained credit assignment using temporal difference (TD) learning on counterfactual trajectories. The counterfactuals are generated by perturbing specific interaction turns within a rollout, while keeping the environment (i.e., the external knowledge source) fixed. The TD learning is then applied to the counterfactual trajectories to derive a reward signal that imputes responsibility to each turn based on the outcomes of alternative trajectories.
CONTROLS: Investigate how the TD reward improves performance and sample efficiency in search tasks compared to learnable embeddings (proposal 1) and progressive history abstraction with goal-oriented selection (revised proposal 2).

However, it may be computationally expensive compared to group-based methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: “Learnable Embeddings for Turn-Level Reward Signals”
PROPOSAL: Design a novel embedding layer that learns to represent the importance and relevance of each interaction turn within a multi-turn search agent trajectory. This embedding would capture the dependencies between turns and weigh the relative contributions of each step toward the final answer. The embedding would be optimized as part of the policy optimization process, allowing the model to automatically adjust its weights to reflect the importance of each turn.

CONTROLS: Evaluate the proposed embedding layer against a standard random baseline, as well as against alternatives that implement hand-crafted heuristics for turn importance.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach is likely to show improved results, especially in terms of distinguishing productive from unproductive turns and providing a more informative reward signal, but may struggle with counterfactual bias and overestimation of turn importance when combined with the outcome reward signal.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: “Progressive History Abstraction”
PROPOSAL: Introduce a history abstraction mechanism that progressively selects and stores relevant intermediate reasoning steps based on their impact on the search trajectory. This abstraction would provide a compact representation of the search agent's history, emphasizing the critical turns that led to the final answer. In subsequent policy updates, the model would rely on this condensed history to focus its exploration and improvement.

CONTROLS: Compare this approach against a baseline where the model stores all turns, as well as against an ablation where only the final answer and its preceding turns are stored.
COST: 170 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should improve sample efficiency by filtering out irrelevant turns and reducing the dimensionality of the model's internal state space, but may struggle with uniformly representing diverse query types and story contexts.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Revised: “Progressive History Abstraction”
PROPOSAL: Revise the progressive history abstraction to incorporate clustering-based aggregation. This would organize intermediate reasoning steps into smaller clusters based on their similarity, and then select cluster representatives as the critical turns in the search history. This clustering-based approach would allow the model to abstract away redundant information and focus on characteristic turns indicative of successful search strategies.

CONTROLS: Evaluate the effectiveness of this revised mechanism against the baseline and ablation mentioned earlier, as well as against a random clustering baseline.
COST: 190 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised approach should benefit from improved generalizability across diverse query types and story contexts, but may increase the risk of over-specialization to specific clusters and local optima.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: “Temporal Difference Credit Assignment”
PROPOSAL: Develop a temporal difference (TD) algorithm adapted for multi-turn search agents, where the TD error is propagated backward through the trajectory to assign credit to each turn based on the importance of its contribution to the final answer. This approach would incorporate aspects of both process and outcome rewards, providing an efficient way to evaluate the value of intermediate reasoning and tool interactions.

CONTROLS: Compare this TD algorithm against the outcome reward baseline, as well as against a simplified ablation that uses only forward TD error updates.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method is likely to show improved performance in distinguishing the impact of individual turns, especially in scenarios with long and complex trajectories, but may struggle with bootstrapping the TD error updates and requiring additional exploration steps.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: “Turn-Level Simulation Oracle”
PROPOSAL: Design a simulation oracle that predicts the effectiveness of each turn in a multi-turn search agent by imagining hypothetical continuation of the current trajectory under different action scenarios. This oracle would allow the model to evaluate potential future actions and assign a turn-level reward based on the predicted outcome.

CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of this simulation oracle against the baseline outcome reward, as well as against ablations that use simplified heuristics or random exploration for simulating the future.
COST: 230 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach is likely to improve the agentic search agent's ability to reason about its own exploration and trajectory planning, but may struggle with accurately simulating complex environments and counterfactual scenarios, and may require significant additional computational resources for oracle updates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: “Greedy State and Action Review”
PROPOSAL: Implement a greedy review mechanism that iteratively evaluates the current state and action taken by the search agent, and selectively revisits or backtracks if the decision appears suboptimal. This process would provide a refinement of the intermediate reasoning process and lead to a denser reward signal.

CONTROLS: Compare this greedy review mechanism against the baseline without review, as well as against an ablation that implements random reward specification.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should improve the search agent's speed and efficiency in providing a denser reward signal by more thoroughly reviewing and refining intermediate turns, but may struggle with quantifying cost or propagating uncertainty in suboptimal decision making.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Revised: “Turn-Level Simulation Oracle”
PROPOSAL: Enhance the simulation oracle to incorporate uncertainty estimation and probabilistic future trajectories. This would allow the model to quantify its confidence in the predicted outcomes and assign rewards based on the sampled likelihood of success. This revised oracle would improve the robustness of the reward signal and allow the model to more accurately evaluate and adapt to uncertainty.

CONTROLS: Evaluate the revised simulation oracle against the original design, as well as against an ablation that uses fixed sampling probabilities and against a baseline without sampling.
COST: 280 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised oracle should significantly improve the search agent's ability to handle uncertainty and adapt to new situations, but may increase the computational overhead due to the need for probabilistic sampling and inference.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: “Attention-Sharing between Turns”
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel attention mechanism that shares attention weights between consecutive turns, enabling the model to effectively weigh and filter contextual information across the intermediate reasoning process. This attention-sharing approach would facilitate the detection of dependencies between turns and allow the model to consolidate relevant knowledge from previous decision-making steps.

CONTROLS: Compare this attention-sharing approach against manual evaluation of relational alignment between turns, as well as against an ablation that uses standard attention mechanisms and separately evaluates each turn.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should improve the search agent's ability to spot relationships between intermediate reasoning steps and contextual knowledge, but may lead to over-reliance on some turns at the expense of others, and may experience difficulty adapting when wonky data fails interpretation.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Revised: “Learnable Embeddings for Turn-Level Reward Signals”
PROPOSAL: Enhance the learnable embeddings approach to incorporate meta-learning, where the model is trained to learn how to adapt and improve its embeddings across different tasks and domains. This meta-learning aspect would enable the embeddings to generalize better across various search scenarios and improve the model's robustness to new situations.

CONTROLS: Evaluate the meta-learning extension against a standard learnable embeddings baseline, as well as against an ablation that trains the embeddings on a single task and domain.
COST: 320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised approach should boost the model's ability to generalize and adapt across different search scenarios, but may experience difficulty identifying key features in the embeddings due to increased parameter space and require additional computational resources for meta-learning updates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: “Concurrent Multitask Reward Inference”
PROPOSAL: Propose a method to leverage the power of multitask learning in agentic search, where the model predicts multiple reward signals in parallel for each turn, and receives training guidance for those predicted rewards. This multitask setup would allow the model to better model the complex relationships between intermediate reasoning steps and reward assignments.

CONTROLS: Evaluate this multitask reward inference approach against a standard baseline and ablations that restrict the model to single-task reward prediction.
COST: 350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should improve the search agent's ability to learn and adapt to diverse reward signals, but may lead to increased computational complexity due to multitask training and require fine-tuning hyperparameters for speed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: “improving outcome-based rewards with stable normalization”
PROPOSAL: Design and evaluate a group normalization variant, where instead of normalizing outcomes within the group, we normalize the advantages in the group. This would ensure the rewards are calculated such that the relative ordering of group outcomes remains preserved, even when identical outcomes occur. To adapt GRPO for this variant, we'll perturb the rollouts in a group slightly so that at least one outcome differs, providing a stable gradient signal.
CONTROLS: Evaluate against baseline GRPO and vanilla outcome-based rewards, using ablation studies to understand the impact of perturbing rollouts.
COST: 5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results show improved robustness to advantage collapse, but could potentially require a higher number of rollouts due to the need for counterfactual outcomes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: “turn distribution-based batch normalization”
PROPOSAL: Introduce a batch normalization method specifically designed for agentic search, focusing on the distribution of turn outcomes within a batch. This is done by comparing the empirical distribution of turn outcomes with a reference distribution. We'll incorporate this normalization into our policy update formula, adapting the loss function used in modern gradient-based optimization techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare our turn distribution-based batch normalization with stable normalization (proposed in previous experiment) and vanilla group-based normalization, assessing its effectiveness in reducing advantage collapse and improving reward signal stability.
COST: 8 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results indicate a moderate improvement in terms of advantage collapse resistance, but may also be subject to over-smoothing of turn outcomes if not properly calibrated; requires adaptive tuning of reference distributions.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: “turn distribution-based batch normalization”
PROPOSAL: Revisit and refine the design of turn distribution-based batch normalization by incorporating a domain-specific prior over turn outcomes. This involves learning or specifying a probability distribution over common outcomes seen during training, such as the echo-turn (the turn where the model simply repeats content from the previous turn), or the non-inflammatory indicative-turn (a turn where the model shows potential, but does not contribute significantly to the conversation). By combining this prior with the batch distribution, we can better adapt the reference distribution and improve overall performance.
CONTROLS: Ablate the prior-based component to demonstrate its contribution. Compare with the non-prior-based version, vanilla group normalization, and the recently introduced stable normalization.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results show a significant improvement in batch normalization robustness to advantage collapse, accompanied by the ability to better utilize rare-but-informative turn outcomes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: “action clustering for content-specific rewards”
PROPOSAL: Introduce a clustering scheme that identifies consistent behavioral patterns in tool-action interactions, particularly in Web search. By grouping similar actions into specific clusters, we assign content-specific rewards that better capture turn-level information, encouraging the policy to express subtle nuances in decision-making. This experiment integrates an unsupervised learning approach using generative models to generate interpretable K-means clustering.
CONTROLS: Assess effect of selectivity in clustering, considering both too fine-grained and too general categorizations. ACTION: ADD 3

ACTION: ADD 4

PROPOSAL: Investigate the potential of emergent interpretability methods (e.g., token attention or feature importance) to provide insight into the quality evaluation process of multilingual quality raters. This'll help identify languages or content types where raters are biased or need improvement, proxying for manual evaluation effort.
CONTROLS: Analyze the emergent interpretations of the rater's internal workings and their alignment with human annotations, and compare to models without emergent interpretability.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (focused on interpretability analysis)
PREDICTION: This approach may reveal masked biases in multilingual quality raters and provide valuable feedback for their improvement but requires careful model selection and interpretability framework implementation.

This proposal focuses on developing techniques that provide transparency and understanding of multilingual quality raters, complementing the assessment of their accuracy.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Active Learning for Multilingual Data Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: Develop an active learning framework for selecting the most informative and representative samples for annotating multilingual data, using uncertainty estimates from the quality rater as a criterion. This'll enable efficient annotation efforts, focusing on high-impact samples, and optimize the performance of the quality rater on diverse languages and tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare to a passive sampling strategy, and to versions with and without uncertainty-based sampling.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (for simulated active learning environment)
PREDICTION: Active learning should enable more efficient multilingual annotation and quality rater improvement, especially in languages with limited annotated data, and help mitigate issues of noise and mislabeling in the human-annotated dataset.

This proposal addresses one of the main bottlenecks in multilingual data quality assessment: the availability of high-quality annotations.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: MetaLearning for Transferable Multilingual Data Quality Raters
PROPOSAL: Explore the application of metalearning (few-shot learning) to develop transferable multilingual quality raters that can adapt to novel languages with minimal human supervision. This'll involve pretraining the rater on a diverse set of languages, followed by fine-tuning on a few examples from the target language.
CONTROLS: Compare to a monolingual rater, and to a standard multitask learning approach.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (requires pretraining and fine-tuning in multiple languages)
PREDICTION: Metalearning has the potential to develop quality raters that generalize across languages, but might require significant computational resources, and the performance may degrade if the few-shot examples are not representative of the target language.

This proposal aims to push the boundaries of language-independence in multilingual quality raters, focusing on leveraging the power of metalearning.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Online Quality Assessment and Self-Adaptation for Multilingual LLM Pretraining
PROPOSAL: Investigate integrating online quality assessment into multilingual LLM pretraining, allowing the quality rater to adapt dynamically based on the emerging dataset. This'll facilitate real-time filtering of low-quality data, adapt to changing data distributions, and potentially improve the overall quality of the pretraining corpus.
CONTROLS: Compare to offline quality assessment, and to a version without self-adaptation.
COST: 800 GPU-hours (for online training and adaptation)
PREDICTION: Online quality assessment and self-adaptation may lead to higher-quality pretraining corpora but risk introducing biases from the rater's own adapting behavior and require careful regularization to prevent overfitting.

This proposal focuses on employing quality assessment as a dynamic component of the pretraining process.

ACTION: ADD 8

CONTROLS: Compare to standard clustering methods (k-means, DBSCAN) and to a version without graph-based clustering.
COST: 400 GPU-hours (for training and evaluation)
PREDICTION: Graph-based clustering methods may offer a data-efficient strategy for identifying high-quality documents but might require careful parameter tuning and choice of similarity metric.

This proposal explores an innovative approach to clustering and evaluating multilingual documents, drawing inspiration from graph theory.

ACTION: ADD 9

PROPOSAL: Perform a comprehensive experimental evaluation of the effect of multifaceted, data-quality-aware multilingual pretraining on the performance of downstream language models (e.g., machine translation, text classification) across various languages and tasks. This final proposal is a comprehensive evaluation of the entire set of proposals, assessing their practical impact on improving downstream model performance via multifaceted, data-quality-aware pretraining strategies.

PROPOSAL: We propose a method called Fusion3D that learns a compact 3D latent representation by combining a signed distance function (SDF) for geometry with a multi-scale, multi-view feature extractor for appearance. TITLE: exploratory meta-learning of adaptive augmentation

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: graph-based optimizer loss entanglement
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel optimizer-loss entanglement method based on graph neural networks (GNNs) to coordinate the optimization process. Represent the optimizer and loss function as nodes in a graph, where edges capture their interactions. Use a GNN to propagate optimizer and loss information across the graph, allowing for joint optimization of the four core components (augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function). Train the GNN using a self-supervised objective that encouragers coordination and synergy among components.
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline where the optimizer and loss are optimized independently, and ablate the graph-based approach to isolate the contribution of the GNN.
COST: Estimated 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should show improved stability and efficiency during training, especially in handling rare labels. However, it may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and might struggle to generalize well to new datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: context-aware multiplicative schedule
PROPOSAL: Introduce a multiplicative learning-rate schedule that adapts to the context of the training process, particularly the progress on each label. Use a contextual-neural-network-based adaptation strategy to adjust the learning-rate multipliers for each label, based on their relative importance and difficulty. This can be implemented using a simple weighted average of standard schedules, where the weights are the outputs of the context-aware neural network.
CONTROLS: Compare to a state-of-the-art adaptive learning-rate schedule (i.e., Cyclical Learning Rate), a fixed schedule such as Step Learning Rate, and a learning rate warm-up without the multiplicative adaptation.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should improve adaptation to rare labels and overall convergence speed, while being simple to implement and requiring relatively few hyperparameters to tune. However, it might not generalize well across different datasets and label distributions.

PROPOSAL: Utilize knowledge distillation to transfer knowledge from an expert teacher model to a student model that adapts its training process to the evolving data distribution. The teacher model is trained on a fixed static configuration, while the student model is trained on an adaptive configuration that learns to mimic the teacher's performance. Use a dynamic distillation loss that considers the changing label interactions and data hardness during training.
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline where the student model is trained independently without knowledge distillation, as well as an ablation study removing the dynamic distillation loss.
COST: Estimated 900 GPU-hours
